results.title: An Advanced Simulation Framework for Sail-Driven Spacecraft Dynamics and Control
results.abstract: The development of spacecrafts with solar and drag sails has gained significant interest in recent years due to their potential for fuel-free propulsion and extended mission lifetimes. This paper begins with a study of current space missions that utilize sail-driven technology, highlighting their applications, challenges, and technological advancements. Based on this analysis, we emphasize the necessity of an accurate and efficient simulation environment for testing and validating control systems designed for solar and drag sail spacecraft, particularly in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), where atmospheric drag plays a crucial role in the disturbance forces. To address this need, we present the implementation of the Drag Deorbit Device (D3) in a CubeSat platform, a propellant-less deployable and controllable drag sail system. Additionally, we propose an advanced Software-in-the-Loop (SIL) simulation framework that overcomes the limitations of previous simulation tools. The presented approach integrates Isaac Sim and Robot Operating System (ROS), leveraging the advantages of physics-based real-time simulation, high-fidelity rendering, and seamless hardware integration. In addition, enhanced GPU-accelerated physics for precise force and torque modeling, modular extensibility for integrating custom spacecraft dynamics, and real-time visualization for intuitive debugging and system analysis is considered. The presented simulation system incorporates orbital perturbations such as gravity gradient effects, atmospheric drag, gravitational anomalies, and forces from relative motion in an elliptical orbit, providing a more realistic operational environment. Instead of relying on predefined mass distribution, this approach applies drag forces directly on the spacecraft’s surface, leveraging the physics engine to naturally resolve the resulting dynamics while maintaining accuracy and enabling seamless adaptation to different spacecraft designs. The proposed SIL architecture follows a digital twin paradigm, ensuring a high-fidelity representation of the spacecraft’s dynamics and control systems within the virtual environment. This digital twin enables rapid prototyping, real-time testing, and iterative refinement of control strategies before deployment in space. By bridging the gap between simulation and real-world implementation, the presented system significantly enhances the reliability and robustness of solar sail spacecraft operations. Through this work, we demonstrate the reliability and accuracy of the proposed system using real data, validating its effectiveness for spacecraft simulation and control in LEO. Additionally, we analyze deorbiting maneuvers to assess the system’s performance in end-of-mission scenarios.
